segments.text: The human mind loves to categorize and rank things.
Review stars for restaurants,
category numbers for hurricanes,
even the size of your T-shirt.
We use them all the time to make sense
of large amounts of information, and make better decisions.
In user experience, we also leverage scales and categories.
When we inspect designs based on heuristics or expertise,
or conduct usability testing,
we discover all sorts of findings.
Instead of simply reporting those findings to your team
as a giant list of grievances,
it's helpful to categorize them on a severity scale.
A severity scale is a relative ranking
based on a finding's estimated harm to user experience.
We can estimate that harm by assigning the finding
a one, two, or three across several factors,
such as how frequently it occurs,
how impactful it is to user experience,
how persistent it can be,
and how detrimental it is to a product's popularity.
Here's a good severity scale to use
when communicating your findings.
It has five ratings.
High severity means the finding contributed
to users stopping their task or resulted in user frustration
or self-blame for struggling with the experience.
Medium severity means users could complete the task,
but with observable frustration, notable slowdown,
or after several attempts.
Low severity means users could complete the task
with just brief slowdown or confusion,
or the findings mostly cosmetic.
Then there are bugs.
No, not the creepy-crawly kind.
This is for when something is not working as intended.
High severity may be true
from a user experience perspective,
but that's a bit unfair to your colleagues.
They didn't want it to work that way either.
So give them the benefit of the doubt
and collaborate with them on documenting
and fixing these bugs.
Finally, there's good,
for findings that aren't problems at all.
Use this rating when something appears
to be consistently beneficial, helpful,
or successful with users.
Sometimes reviewing these findings can be demoralizing,
but that's a natural human reaction to negative feedback.
But all user experiences have good and bad aspects to them.
Be sure to remind your team what's working well, too.
Use these ratings to arrange your findings
starting with high severity to low,
with a few good, and bugs, mixed in between.
If presenting the findings to your team,
label each finding's severity clearly
and have a slide in the back of the presentation
for the scale for reference.
By using this simple scale,
you'll communicate more effectively with your team or stakeholders.
They'll quickly understand a finding's impact
and make informed decisions about priorities and resourcing.
And if you consistently use the same severity scale,
your colleagues will eventually learn it
and trust it over time.
And I rate that outcome five stars.
